title: Fading, polarization and absorption
blurb: Explain why signals fade, why antennas must match polarization, and what absorbs or reflects them.

T3A01.why: Direct and reflected waves arrive out of step. A few feet of movement flips them between **cancelling** and **reinforcing**.

T3A02.why: Leaves and branches **absorb** short UHF and microwave waves, so weak signals get weaker.

T3A03.why: Weak-signal CW and SSB work on VHF/UHF uses **horizontal** polarization by convention.
T3A03.trap: Vertical is for FM and repeaters; circular is used for satellites.

T3A04.why: Crossed antennas no longer line up with the electric field, so **received signal strength drops**.

T3A05.why: With the direct path blocked, find a **reflecting path** (a building or hill) and aim the antenna at it.
T3A05.trap: Changing polarization does not clear an obstruction.

T3A06.why: Picket fencing is the **rapid flutter** of a mobile signal as the car passes through multipath peaks and nulls.

T3A07.why: Rain and other **precipitation** absorb microwaves, shortening range.
T3A07.trap: Wind, cold and pressure changes don't absorb microwaves.

T3A08.why: Signals via the ionosphere take several paths and **combine randomly**, so strength fades irregularly.

T3A09.why: Ionospheric signals arrive **elliptically** polarized, so **either** vertical or horizontal antennas work.
T3A09.trap: Matching polarization matters on line-of-sight paths, not via the ionosphere.

T3A10.why: Delayed copies of the signal smear the data, so **error rates increase**.

T3A11.why: The **ionosphere** reflects (refracts) HF waves back to Earth.
T3A11.trap: The troposphere is the weather layer; the "electrosphere" isn't a thing.

T3A12.why: At 10 m and 6 m the waves are long, so fog and rain have **little effect**.
T3A12.trap: Absorption by water is a UHF and microwave problem.
